summary: This program stores the value of pi in two decimal types \  64-bit double, prints both, then adds them and converts the double back down to a float. It shows how Java handles decimal numbers of different sizes and what happens when you squeeze the larger one into the smaller one.

lines.text: The trailing f is required: Java treats every decimal literal as a double by default, so without it the compiler refuses to put 3.14 into a float variable.
A double has room for roughly twice as many significant digits, which is why it is the usual choice for calculations where precision loss matters.

lines.code: double sum = f + d;              // float promoted to double
lines.text: When a float and a double are added, Java widens the float to a double automatically and the result is a double \ no cast needed, because nothing can be lost going up in size.

lines.code: float narrowed = (float) d;      // explicit cast from double to float
lines.text: Going the other direction discards digits, so Java makes you write the cast to confirm you accept the loss.
Compare this line's output with the printed double: the tail of pi is simply gone, which is narrowing precision loss you can see.
